full_judgment:
The plaintiff's further case was that for arrear of rent, certificate cases were started against the heirs of S.A. recorded tenants and the suit property was sold in auction and the plaintiff being the highest bidder in open auction purchased it on 22-1-71 and the sale was confirmed on 23-12-72, the certificate was granted in favour of the plaintiff on 24-12-72 and the certificate officer formally delivered possession of the property to the plaintiff on 28-12-72. Thereafter Mihir Kumar Saha one of the vendors of the plaintiff filed an application for setting aside the said sale, which was ultimately withdrawn on 18-5-72 and as a result the auction sale remained confirmed. 

 2. Pursuant to the said Bainanama dated 4-3-65 the plaintiff's vendors executed the Kabala which was registered on 19-5-72. Thus the plaintiff became -/16/- annas owner and possessor in the suit property and accordingly paid rent and mutated his name in the record of rights as well as in the Paurashava. 

 4. Two sets of written-statements were filed by defendant no. 1 and the Government. In the written-statement filed by defendant no. 1, it was alleged that some of the recorded persons left for India long before 1965 and the suit property being the enemy property vested upon the Government under the provisions of Ordinance No.1 of 1964 and that Sukumar Saha Roy and Mihir Kumar Saha Roy were not in possession of the suit property and one Hari Mohan was the authorised person as caretaker of the suit property, who inducted defendant no.1 in the suit property as a monthly tenant and then the said Hari Mohan left for India. Subsequently, the said Sukumar Saha Roy sold his share to Amena who in her turn transferred the same to one Kuddus Dewan and others and the share of Mihir Kumar Saha Roy was also transferred to Nasiruddin and others. Defendant no.1 after liberation of Bangladesh being aware of the suit property as enemy property applied for lease and was in possession but as his brother was killed he fled away from the suit property and during his absence, the plaintiff forcibly entered into the suit property and thereafter on 25-4-74, the defendant No.1 applied for lease of the suit property and the impugned memorandum was passed causing eviction of the plaintiff. 

 10. The trial Court found plaintiff's title to the disputed land on the basis of purchase by Kabala executed by Mihir Kumar Saha Roy and Sukumar Saha Roy but held that the alleged auction sale and purchase was illegal as some dead persons were made parties in that certificate sale and that necessary person were not made parties. The plaintiff was found in possession of the disputed property. The lower appellate Court took the view that the plaintiff's Kabala was hit by Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 and as such plaintiff did not acquire any title on the disputed land on the basis of Kabala executed by Mihir Kumar Saha Roy and Sukumar Saha Roy. It however found plaintiff's possession and title on the basis of auction purchase. The lower appellate Court observed; "custodian cannot take without filing a suit for partition of the portion which has been declared as enemy property. In view of what I have discussed above I cannot but hold that the learned Munsif has rightly decreed the suit and I see no reason to interfere with his judgment". The learned Judge of the High Court Division though found possession in favour of the plaintiff however observed "so far auction purchase is concerned the trial Court held that the certificate being against some dead persons is nullity and the certificate sale is illegal and void. The lower appellate Court did not reverse the findings and decision of the trial Court in this respect after considering the evidence on record. There is therefore error apparent on the face of the record in the judgment and decree passed by the lower appellate Court". Accordingly, he set aside the said judgment and decree and sent back the appeal in remand to the lower appellate Court for re-hearing and disposal in accordance with law and in the light of the observations made in the judgment. While sending the case on remand the learned Judge further observed "it will have to be seen whether plaintiff is entitled to the declaration without proving his legal right or character to the suit land". 

 12. In that view of the matter, we find substance in the contention of the learned Counsel for the appellant that the Kabala in favour of the plaintiff being executed on 3-5-72 and registered on 19-5-72, is not hit by the provision of Ordinance No. 1 of 1964. There is also substance in the contention of the learned Counsel for the appellant that since the Government did not move the High Court Divisi6n against dismissal of their Appeal No. 202 of 1978, the Government accepted the position that the impugned Memorandum issued by Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) is illegal and void. Mr. Maksudur Rahman, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, appearing on behalf of respondents 2 to 8, however, submits that although the Government did not move the High Court Division against the judgment of the lower appellate Court dismissing their appeal but the Government was made a party in Civil Revision No. 1419 of 1980 filed by defendant no.1 and the appearance of the learned Advocate for the Government was noted in the judgment. This appearance, however, does not alter the position. The lower appellate Court, although on a ground different from that of the trial Court, found prima facie title of the plaintiff in the suit land and as such there was no justification for the learned Judge of the High Court Division to observe that it would have to be seen whether plaintiff was entitled to the declaration without proving his legal right or character to the suit land. All the Courts below including the High Court Division found plaintiff in possession of the disputed land. The trial Court decreed plaintiff's suit and the lower appellate Court affirmed the decree although on a different ground. As it is found that plaintiff's Kabala is not hit by Ordinance No. 1 of 1964, plaintiff's title on the basis of purchase by Kabala has been well established and there is no reason to send the case back on remand to the lower appellate Court. The learned Judge of the High Court Division has not exercised his discretion judicially in remanding the case. There is no error of law apparent on the face of the record nor has any failure of justice been occasioned by the decision of the lower appellate Court.
